document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever and progressive swelling of the right eyelid that began after several days of nasal congestion. The lid is severely swollen, the conjunctiva is injected with marked chemosis, and the globe is proptosed. He resists eye movement because of pain, ocular motility is reduced, and vision in that eye is diminished with intermittent double vision. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Internal hordeolum of the upper lid

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes contrasts preseptal and orbital cellulitis: proptosis, conjunctival injection, marked chemosis, pain on eye movement, decreased ocular mobility, and diminished vision with diplopia are features of orbital cellulitis, while all of these are absent or only mild in preseptal disease. This child has fever plus the full orbital constellation, and sinusitis is a listed associated finding, so infection has extended posterior to the orbital septum.

optionExplanations.a: In preseptal cellulitis proptosis, chemosis, pain on eye movement and reduced vision are absent and ocular motility is normal.
optionExplanations.b: Dacryocystitis produces a tender swelling over the lacrimal sac medially, not proptosis with restricted painful motility.
optionExplanations.d: A hordeolum is a localized lid lesion and does not cause proptosis, decreased motility or diminished vision.
optionExplanations.e: Allergic disease causes itch and lid edema without fever, proptosis, painful motility or vision loss.

source.reference: OP10 — Clinical Features of Preseptal and Orbital Cellulitis

questions.question: A 24-year-old teacher has a 3-day history of a red, watery right eye with lid swelling and a gritty sensation; the left eye became involved yesterday. She had a sore throat last week. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye, the cornea is clear, there are follicles on the tarsal conjunctiva, and a tender preauricular node is palpable. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Topical corticosteroid drops four times daily
Cool compresses, topical lubrication, and strict hand hygiene advice
Topical mast cell stabilizer such as olopatadine

questions.explanation: Serous (watery) discharge, follicles, a tender preauricular node, an associated sore throat, and spread to the fellow eye within a few days describe adenoviral conjunctivitis. Toronto Notes states it is usually self-limiting over 7-12 days and is treated with cool compresses and topical lubrication, with proper hygiene to prevent transmission since it is highly contagious for up to 12 days.

optionExplanations.a: Topical steroids are listed for allergic, atopic and giant papillary conjunctivitis, not for routine viral conjunctivitis.
optionExplanations.c: Mast cell stabilizers treat allergic conjunctivitis, which causes pruritus with mucoid discharge and papillae rather than follicles and a tender node.
optionExplanations.d: Intramuscular ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis, which produces hyperpurulent discharge.
optionExplanations.e: Oral azithromycin is used for chlamydial and inclusion conjunctivitis, which is chronic with mucopurulent discharge.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis reports 5 days of severe deep, boring pain in the left eye that wakes her at night and radiates across her face. She has photophobia and her vision has dropped to 20/60. The globe is diffusely red with a violaceous hue best appreciated in daylight, and the injected vessels do not blanch 15 minutes after a drop of phenylephrine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes scleritis as severe deep or boring pain that may awaken the patient at night, with photophobia, red eye and decreased vision, a purple or violaceous hue from scleral thinning exposing the uvea, and failure to blanch with topical phenylephrine. Collagen vascular disease such as rheumatoid arthritis is a listed etiology, and anterior scleritis characteristically radiates to the face.

optionExplanations.a: Episcleral vessels blanch with topical phenylephrine and episcleritis causes discomfort rather than boring night pain with vision loss.
optionExplanations.b: Anterior uveitis produces ciliary flush, miosis, and anterior chamber cells and flare rather than a violaceous non-blanching scleral hue.
optionExplanations.c: Bacterial conjunctivitis causes purulent discharge, papillae and chemosis without deep boring pain or reduced acuity.
optionExplanations.e: Herpes simplex keratitis gives a fluorescein-staining dendritic epithelial lesion with corneal hypoesthesia, not diffuse violaceous scleral injection.

questions.question: A 22-year-old student who regularly sleeps in her soft contact lenses has 2 days of increasing pain, photophobia, tearing and blurred vision in the left eye. Visual acuity is 20/200. The cornea shows a white, necrotic-appearing excavated lesion with an infiltrative base and an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein. There is marked conjunctival injection and a small hypopyon. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Urgent ophthalmology referral, corneal culture before treatment, then intense fortified topical antibiotics hourly
Pressure patch the eye and provide topical anesthetic drops for pain
Topical corticosteroid drops to reduce the infiltrate
Preservative-free artificial tears and review in one week

questions.explanation: An excavated corneal opacity with an infiltrative base, epithelial defect, injection and hypopyon in a contact lens wearer is a corneal ulcer; contact lens use accounts for about half of ulcers. Toronto Notes directs urgent referral to ophthalmology, culture prior to treatment, and intense fortified topical antibiotics hourly, treating vigorously to avoid perforation, iritis and endophthalmitis.

optionExplanations.b: Patching is contraindicated in contact lens wearers because it can precipitate infection, and topical anesthetics must never be prescribed for treatment.
optionExplanations.c: Topical steroids impair corneal healing and are not the initial management of an infectious ulcer.
optionExplanations.d: Antivirals and debridement are for herpes simplex dendritic keratitis, which shows a branching lesion with terminal end bulbs, not a necrotic excavated ulcer.
optionExplanations.e: Lubrication alone risks corneal perforation and endophthalmitis in a suspected infectious ulcer.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man reports 2 years of gradual, painless blurring of vision in both eyes. He is bothered by glare and by halos around oncoming headlights at night, and he occasionally sees two overlapping images even with one eye covered. He has noticed he can now read small print without his usual glasses. The eyes are white and painless, and the view of the retina on fundoscopy is hazy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists the features of cataract as a gradual, painless, progressive decrease in visual acuity with glare, dimness, halos around lights at night and monocular diplopia, and notes the 'second sight' myopic shift seen with nuclear sclerosis, in which increased lens refractive power makes the patient more myopic so near vision improves. A cataract may also impair the view of the retina during fundoscopy.

optionExplanations.a: Open-angle glaucoma causes painless loss of peripheral vision and does not produce a myopic shift or a hazy fundus view.
optionExplanations.b: Dry macular degeneration causes progressive central vision loss without glare, halos, monocular diplopia or an obscured fundus view.
optionExplanations.d: Presbyopia worsens near vision requiring reading glasses; it does not improve unaided near vision or blur the retinal view.
optionExplanations.e: Macular edema from diabetes reduces central acuity but does not cause monocular diplopia, halos or an opacified media with second sight.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents 45 minutes after sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in the right eye. He recalls a similar episode lasting a few minutes last month. Visual acuity is light perception only, there is a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopy shows a pale edematous retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula and a glistening plaque at an arteriolar bifurcation. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Topical prostaglandin analogue and review in 48 hours
Observation, since the deficit is likely to recover spontaneously
Digital ocular massage with measures to lower intraocular pressure while arranging emergency ophthalmology assessment

questions.explanation: A cherry-red spot with retinal edema, a relative afferent pupillary defect, prior amaurosis fugax and a Hollenhorst plaque indicate central retinal artery occlusion. Toronto Notes calls this an ocular emergency in which blood flow must be restored within 2 hours, since complete occlusion beyond about 90 minutes causes irreversible retinal damage. Immediate measures are globe massage to dislodge the embolus and lowering intraocular pressure with a topical beta-blocker, IV acetazolamide, IV mannitol or anterior chamber paracentesis.

optionExplanations.a: Anti-VEGF injection is used for neovascular macular disease and macular edema, not to reperfuse an occluded retinal artery.
optionExplanations.b: Pan-retinal photocoagulation treats proliferative retinal neovascularization and does nothing for acute arterial occlusion.
optionExplanations.c: A single topical agent with delayed review wastes the narrow 2-hour window for restoring retinal perfusion.
optionExplanations.d: Observation guarantees irreversible damage; this presentation is an ocular emergency requiring immediate treatment.

questions.question: A 64-year-old highly myopic woman describes 1 day of flashing lights and a shower of new floaters in the right eye, followed by a curtain of blackness spreading across her temporal field. Central acuity is still 20/25. Intraocular pressure is 5 mmHg lower than in the fellow eye, there is a subtle relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopy shows an elevated grey-white area of retina with loss of the red reflex in that sector. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Exudative retinal detachment from a choroidal tumour

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes retinal detachment as sudden onset of flashes from mechanical stimulation of photoreceptors, floaters from blood released by torn vessels, and a curtain of blackness corresponding to the detached retina, with intraocular pressure usually 4-5 mmHg lower than the fellow eye, a possible relative afferent pupillary defect, and a grey-white detached retina with loss of red reflex. The rhegmatogenous type is the most common and its incidence rises with advancing age and in high myopes.

optionExplanations.a: Isolated vitreous hemorrhage obscures the fundus diffusely rather than producing a discrete elevated grey-white retina with a sectoral field curtain.
optionExplanations.c: Vein occlusion causes painless vision loss with diffuse retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, venous engorgement and a swollen disc.
optionExplanations.d: Exudative detachment arises from intraocular tumour, posterior uveitis or central serous retinopathy and is not preceded by flashes and floaters from a retinal tear.
optionExplanations.e: Posterior uveitis is painless with vitreous cells and opacities, not an acute peripheral field curtain with lowered intraocular pressure.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman who smokes reports 3 weeks of worsening central vision in the right eye; straight door frames now appear wavy. Acuity is 20/80 on the right and 20/25 on the left, and Amsler grid testing confirms central distortion. Fluorescein angiography shows pathologic new vessels leaking dye beneath the macula, and OCT demonstrates intraretinal and subretinal exudation. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Antioxidant supplementation with monitoring using an Amsler grid
Low vision aids such as magnifiers and closed-circuit television
Intravitreal injection of an anti-VEGF agent
Sunglasses and increased dietary green leafy vegetables

questions.explanation: Metamorphopsia with central vision loss plus angiographic leakage from choroidal neovascularization indicates neovascular ('wet') age-related macular degeneration; smoking, female sex and increasing age are listed risk factors. Toronto Notes gives intravitreal anti-VEGF injection (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept, brolucizumab, faricimab) as the treatment for neovascular AMD, with photodynamic therapy as an alternative option.

optionExplanations.a: Antioxidants and Amsler grid monitoring are the management of non-neovascular 'dry' AMD, not of active choroidal neovascularization.
optionExplanations.b: Low vision aids are supportive measures for dry AMD and do not treat leaking new vessels.
optionExplanations.c: Fundus autofluorescence is an imaging tool used to monitor progression of dry AMD, not a treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Sunglasses and dietary measures are listed under dry AMD management and will not halt exudative disease.

questions.question: A 68-year-old hyperopic woman develops severe right eye pain, frontal headache, nausea and vomiting after sitting for 2 hours in a dark cinema. She sees halos around lights and her vision is acutely blurred. The eye is red, the cornea is hazy, the pupil is fixed and mid-dilated, the anterior chamber is shallow, and the globe feels hard on palpation. After medical therapy lowers the pressure, which is the definitive treatment?

options.text: Serial intraocular pressure checks with no further intervention

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes acute angle-closure glaucoma as a red painful eye with decreased vision blurred by corneal edema, halos, nausea and vomiting, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior chamber and marked pressure rise palpable as a hard globe; hyperopia, age over 70, female sex and pupil dilation in darkness are risk factors. Medical therapy uses aqueous suppressants, hyperosmotic agents and pilocarpine to reverse pupillary block, but laser iridotomy is the definitive treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Prostaglandin analogues are chronic open-angle glaucoma therapy and do not relieve pupillary block.
optionExplanations.c: Trabeculectomy is a filtering procedure for glaucoma refractory to other measures, not the definitive treatment of acute angle closure.
optionExplanations.d: Pan-retinal photocoagulation treats retinal ischemia and neovascularization, a different mechanism of secondary glaucoma.
optionExplanations.e: Observation risks irreversible vision loss within hours to days and permanent peripheral anterior synechiae.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes undergoes a dilated retinal examination. Acuity is 20/25 in each eye. There are microaneurysms with dot and blot hemorrhages in all four quadrants, scattered hard exudates, several cotton-wool spots, and dilated non-leaking intraretinal collateral vessels in the superotemporal quadrant. No new vessels are seen on the disc, retina or iris, and there is no vitreous hemorrhage. How is this retinopathy best classified?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy by hard exudates, dot and blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms and retinal edema, and defines advanced or pre-proliferative disease as these findings plus intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (dilated, non-leaky collateral vessels) in one of four quadrants, hemorrhages with microvascular anomalies in all four quadrants, and nerve fibre layer infarcts (cotton-wool spots). This patient has exactly those additional features without any neovascularization.

optionExplanations.a: Mild non-proliferative disease lacks intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, four-quadrant hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots.
optionExplanations.b: Proliferative disease requires neovascularization of the iris, disc or retina, which is explicitly absent here.
optionExplanations.d: Macular edema is defined by retinal thickening at or within 500 micrometres of the macular centre; acuity is preserved and no macular thickening is described.
optionExplanations.e: The findings and the diabetic history fit diabetic retinopathy; grade 3 hypertensive change requires obvious arterial narrowing with focal irregularities plus hemorrhages or exudate.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man has 3 days of a painful, red left eye with marked photophobia and mildly blurred vision. There is no discharge. Visual acuity is 20/40 on the left. The injection is perilimbal, the left pupil is smaller than the right, keratic precipitates are seen on the corneal endothelium, and there are cells and flare in the anterior chamber. Intraocular pressure is 12 mmHg and he has no nausea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes' table of common differential diagnoses of red eye separates the causes by discharge, pupil, injection pattern, cornea and IOP. Acute iritis has no discharge, dull achy pain with marked photophobia, ciliary flush (perilimbal injection), a smaller pupil, keratic precipitates, cells and flare in the anterior chamber, and no nausea or vomiting. This man's findings match that column exactly.

optionExplanations.b: Viral conjunctivitis produces serous or mucoid discharge with diffuse conjunctival injection, a normal pupil, no photophobia and no anterior chamber cells.
optionExplanations.c: Bacterial conjunctivitis gives purulent discharge with diffuse conjunctival injection, a normal pupil and normal intraocular pressure.
optionExplanations.d: Acute glaucoma causes a markedly increased intraocular pressure with a cloudy cornea, a pupil fixed in mid-dilation, coloured haloes and nausea and vomiting.
optionExplanations.e: Keratitis with a corneal ulcer shows a corneal infiltrate with edema and purulent discharge if bacterial, rather than a clear cornea with keratic precipitates alone.

source.reference: OP4 — Common Differential Diagnoses of Red Eye

questions.question: A 32-year-old man reports 3 weeks of painless blurred vision with floaters in both eyes. Over the past 2 years he has had recurrent oral ulcers and genital ulcers. Visual acuity is 20/80 bilaterally. There is no conjunctival or scleral injection and the anterior chambers are quiet, but posterior segment examination shows vitreous cells and opacities with patches of chorioretinal inflammation. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies uveitis anatomically: posterior uveitis is painless, often has no conjunctival or scleral injection, and presents with decreased visual acuity, floaters, and vitreous cells and opacities with inflammation of the choroid and retina. Among the autoimmune causes listed, Behcet's disease is defined by the triad of oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and posterior uveitis, which is precisely this man's presentation.

optionExplanations.a: Sarcoidosis is listed as a secondary cause of intermediate uveitis and can cause granulomatous inflammation, but it is not associated with recurrent oral and genital ulcers.
optionExplanations.c: Ankylosing spondylitis is an HLA-B27 associated cause of anterior uveitis, which presents with photophobia, ocular pain and ciliary flush rather than painless vitreous inflammation.
optionExplanations.d: Toxoplasmosis is the most common parasitic cause of posterior uveitis but does not produce recurrent oral and genital ulceration.
optionExplanations.e: Syphilis is a bacterial cause of posterior uveitis; its ulcers are painless genital chancres and it lacks the recurrent oral ulcer triad.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye that began this morning, preceded by a shower of many floaters. Visual acuity is hand motion. The eye is white and painless and the pupil reacts to light. On direct ophthalmoscopy there is no red reflex and the retina cannot be visualized. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists proliferative diabetic retinopathy first among the etiologies of vitreous hemorrhage, which causes sudden loss of visual acuity that may be preceded by a shower of many floaters and/or flashes of light. On ophthalmoscopy there is no red reflex if the hemorrhage is large and the retina is not visible because of blood in the vitreous. B-scan ultrasound is then used to rule out retinal detachment.

optionExplanations.a: Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes but does not obliterate the red reflex or reduce acuity to hand motion.
optionExplanations.b: Retinal detachment is a listed cause of vitreous hemorrhage, but detachment alone leaves the red reflex intact and the retina visible on ophthalmoscopy.
optionExplanations.d: A dislocated lens produces decreased acuity with monocular diplopia, iridodonesis and phacodonesis, and an abnormal rather than absent red reflex.
optionExplanations.e: Retinal vein occlusion is listed as a cause of vitreous hemorrhage, but by itself the fundus remains visible.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man of African descent is asymptomatic but is found at a screening visit to have intraocular pressures of 24 mmHg in both eyes, with a vertical cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 on the right and 0.4 on the left. His mother had glaucoma. Which of the following additional findings would constitute another major risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes divides primary open-angle glaucoma risk factors into major and minor. The major risk factors are ocular hypertension (IOP >21 mmHg), age, African descent, family history, and a thin central cornea as shown in the OHTS trial. Myopia, hypertension, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, chronic corticosteroid use and previous ocular trauma are listed as minor risk factors. This man already has elevated IOP, African descent, a family history and an increased vertical cup-to-disc ratio with asymmetry between the eyes.

optionExplanations.a: Myopia is listed among the minor risk factors for primary open-angle glaucoma.
optionExplanations.b: Hypertension appears only under the minor risk factors.
optionExplanations.c: Diabetes mellitus is listed as a minor risk factor.
optionExplanations.e: Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) is listed as a minor risk factor.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with migraines and sleep apnea is referred for progressive optic disc cupping. Examination shows notching of the neuroretinal rim in both eyes and arcuate scotomas on visual field testing. Gonioscopy shows open angles. Intraocular pressure measured at several different times of day ranges from 15 to 18 mmHg. She has never used topical or systemic steroids and has no history of ocular trauma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines normal tension glaucoma as glaucomatous optic neuropathy with IOP in the normal range, often found in women over 60, and associated with migraines, peripheral vasospasm, systemic nocturnal hypotension and sleep apnea, with optic nerve damage attributed to vascular insufficiency. This woman has rim notching and arcuate scotomas, which are characteristic glaucomatous findings, yet her IOP never exceeds the normal range.

optionExplanations.a: Primary open-angle glaucoma is characterized by an insidious, painless, gradual rise in IOP; her pressures remain in the normal range.
optionExplanations.c: In angle-closure the peripheral iris bows forward and obstructs the trabecular meshwork, whereas gonioscopy here shows open angles.
optionExplanations.d: Steroid-induced glaucoma requires exposure to topical, periocular, systemic or inhaled steroids, which she has never used.
optionExplanations.e: Pigmentary glaucoma results from pigment dispersion syndrome with iris pigment deposited in the trabecular meshwork, and typically raises IOP.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has noticed for 2 weeks that her right pupil is larger than the left. There is no ptosis, eye movements are full and visual acuity is normal. The right pupil is irregular, reacts poorly to light but constricts slowly to a near target, and the anisocoria is greater in bright light. One drop of dilute pilocarpine 0.125% constricts the right pupil but has no effect on the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes' summary of conditions causing anisocoria describes Adie's tonic pupil as an irregular pupil that is larger in bright light, from a lesion in the ciliary ganglion, reacting poorly to light but better to accommodation, with anisocoria greater in light. Denervation hypersensitivity means a dilute (0.125%) solution of pilocarpine constricts the tonic pupil but has no effect on a normal pupil, which is exactly what happened here.

optionExplanations.b: In CN III palsy the pupil is round and fixed acutely at 7-9 mm, with ptosis and the eye deviated down and out; her lids and motility are normal.
optionExplanations.c: Horner's syndrome is an abnormal miotic pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis, and the anisocoria is greater in dark rather than in light.
optionExplanations.d: Argyll-Robertson pupils are miotic and usually bilateral from a midbrain lesion, not a unilateral mydriatic pupil.
optionExplanations.e: A pharmacologically dilated pupil is round, fixed at 7-8 mm and will not constrict with pilocarpine.

source.reference: OP31 — Summary of Conditions Causing Anisocoria

questions.question: A 47-year-old man has 3 days of left-sided neck pain and a drooping left upper eyelid. The left pupil measures 2 mm and the right 4 mm, the difference being greater in dim light, and both react briskly to light. There is reduced sweating over the left side of his face. Extraocular movements are full and visual acuity is normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Urgent imaging of the carotid arteries
Chest imaging to look for a Pancoast tumour
MRI of the brainstem for a lateral medullary infarct

questions.explanation: Miosis, anhidrosis and ptosis with anisocoria greater in dim light define Horner's syndrome. Toronto Notes lists its causes as mostly idiopathic, with brainstem infarct (lateral medullary syndrome), Pancoast tumour, neck surgery and carotid artery dissection, and states explicitly that carotid artery dissection must be ruled out in an acute Horner's syndrome less than 14 days old. His neck pain and 3-day history make this the priority.

optionExplanations.b: Cocaine confirms the diagnosis pharmacologically but is rarely used in practice because of availability, and it does not identify the life-threatening cause.
optionExplanations.c: Hydroxyamphetamine localizes the lesion to a preganglionic or postganglionic site but is not available in Canada or the USA.
optionExplanations.d: Pancoast tumour is a recognized cause but is not the urgent consideration in an acute Horner's syndrome with ipsilateral neck pain.
optionExplanations.e: A brainstem infarct is a listed cause, but it would be expected to produce other neurologic findings and does not take priority over excluding dissection.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman has 5 days of progressively blurred vision in the right eye. Colour vision is markedly decreased in that eye, there is a central scotoma, and a right relative afferent pupillary defect is present. The fundus is otherwise unremarkable. MRI demonstrates white matter demyelinating lesions of the right optic nerve. What is the best initial treatment for her optic neuritis?

options.text: IV corticosteroids with a taper to oral form

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists blurred vision with decreased colour vision from optic neuritis, a central scotoma from damage to the papillomacular bundle, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and white matter demyelinating lesions of the optic nerve on MRI as ocular features of multiple sclerosis. The stated treatment for optic neuritis is IV steroids with a taper to the oral form, and oral steroids must not be given in isolation because of the increased risk of developing multiple sclerosis.

optionExplanations.a: Toronto Notes states explicitly that optic neuritis should not be treated with oral steroids in isolation because of the increased risk of developing multiple sclerosis.
optionExplanations.c: Topical corticosteroid drops do not reach the optic nerve and are used for anterior segment inflammation.
optionExplanations.d: There is no infectious cause here; the MRI shows demyelinating lesions of the optic nerve.
optionExplanations.e: Withholding treatment forgoes the recommended IV steroid course with oral taper for optic neuritis.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman awoke with painless loss of vision in the left eye. For 3 weeks she has had headache with tenderness over the temporal artery and constitutional symptoms. CBC shows thrombocytosis and both ESR and CRP are markedly elevated. Giant cell arteritis is suspected clinically. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Arrange temporal artery biopsy and withhold treatment until the result is available
Start high dose corticosteroids immediately and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Start low dose acetylsalicylic acid and repeat inflammatory markers in 1 week
Refer for carotid Doppler ultrasound before starting any treatment
Observe and reassess if the fellow eye becomes involved

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that if a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis is suspected clinically, STAT treatment should be started and a temporal artery biopsy performed to confirm the diagnosis within 2 weeks of the initial presentation. High dose corticosteroids are given to prevent further ischemic complications and to improve systemic symptoms. Her thrombocytosis with elevated ESR and CRP supports the diagnosis, and treatment must not wait for the biopsy.

optionExplanations.a: Delaying steroids until biopsy results are available risks further ischemic complications; biopsy can still confirm the diagnosis within 2 weeks of presentation.
optionExplanations.c: Acetylsalicylic acid and repeat blood work do not prevent further ischemic damage in giant cell arteritis.
optionExplanations.d: Carotid imaging does not diagnose giant cell arteritis and delays the definitive corticosteroid treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Observation is unacceptable because untreated giant cell arteritis carries a very high risk of ischemic complications.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl who has never worn glasses fails a preschool vision screen. Visual acuity is 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. The eyes are straight on cover and cover-uncover testing, the media are clear and the fundi are normal. Cycloplegic refraction shows +4.00 D in the right eye and +0.50 D in the left. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Spectacle correction of the refractive error
Immediate part-time occlusion patching of the left eye
Atropine penalization of the left eye
Strabismus surgery on the right eye

questions.explanation: This is anisometropic amblyopia: asymmetric refractive errors with reduced best-corrected acuity in the more hyperopic eye and no strabismus or structural abnormality. Toronto Notes states that anisometropia is treated with glasses to correct the refractive error, and that patching or atropine is required only if a visual acuity difference persists after using glasses for 3-6 months. Treatment is most effective in early childhood, so she should be started now.

optionExplanations.b: Occlusion therapy is reserved for a persisting acuity difference after 3-6 months of spectacle wear, and over-treatment risks reverse amblyopia in the better-seeing eye.
optionExplanations.c: Atropine penalization of the good eye is an alternative to patching but, like patching, follows a trial of glasses in anisometropia.
optionExplanations.d: Her eyes are straight on cover testing, so there is no strabismus to operate on.
optionExplanations.e: Toronto Notes states there is no proven value for vision therapy or training in the treatment of strabismus or amblyopia.

questions.question: A 16-month-old boy, born at term, is brought in because his left pupil appeared white in recent family photographs. On direct ophthalmoscopy the red reflex is absent on the left, and that eye turns inward. Dilated fundus examination of the left eye shows nodular, cream-coloured masses with intralesional blood vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leukocoria is a white pupillary reflex with an absent red reflex and warrants urgent referral to an ophthalmologist. Toronto Notes states that retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children, often presents with leukocoria and/or strabismus, and that fundus examination shows nodular, white or cream-coloured masses with intralesional blood vessels. B-scan ultrasound or MRI may demonstrate a calcified mass.

optionExplanations.a: Cataract is in the differential of leukocoria but opacifies the lens rather than producing a vascularized retinal mass.
optionExplanations.b: Coats disease is exudative retinal telangiectasis and does not produce nodular cream-coloured masses with intralesional vessels.
optionExplanations.d: Persistent fetal vasculature causes leukocoria from retrolental tissue, not a nodular retinal tumour.
optionExplanations.e: Retinopathy of prematurity requires prematurity and low birth weight; this child was born at term.

questions.question: A 26-year-old construction worker splashed liquid drain cleaner, an alkali, into his right eye 10 minutes ago. He has severe pain and blepharospasm and the cornea appears hazy. He arrives in the emergency department holding the eye shut and no irrigation has been performed. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Immediate copious irrigation with water or balanced saline solution until physiologic pH is reached
Instillation of a dilute acid to neutralize the alkali
Topical antibiotic ointment and patching of the eye
Topical corticosteroid drops to reduce inflammation
Topical cycloplegic drops to relieve iris spasm

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes directs immediate irrigation with water or balanced saline solution for chemical burns, with the eyelids retracted and an IV drip run until physiologic pH is reached, tested with litmus paper, followed by swabbing the upper and lower fornices to remove particulate matter. Alkali burns carry a worse prognosis than acid burns and can progress for weeks even when the cornea initially looks clear, so irrigation must not be delayed.

optionExplanations.b: Toronto Notes states not to attempt to neutralize an acid with a base or vice versa.
optionExplanations.c: Topical antibiotics and patching are part of subsequent treatment but come after irrigation to physiologic pH.
optionExplanations.d: Topical steroids are prescribed by an ophthalmologist later to decrease inflammation, and are not the immediate step.
optionExplanations.e: Cycloplegics decrease iris spasm and help prevent secondary glaucoma, but they follow irrigation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man has 4 days of burning pain and a vesicular rash over his left forehead and upper eyelid that is unilateral and respects the midline, with vesicles on the tip of his nose. The left eye is red and tearing with photophobia. Slit-lamp examination shows corneal edema with a pseudodendrite and SPK, and corneal sensation is reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus occurs from reactivation of latent herpes zoster virus and produces dermatitis in the dermatomal distribution of CN V1 that is typically unilateral and respects the midline, with pain, tearing, photophobia, red eye, corneal edema, pseudodendrite, SPK, and corneal hypoesthesia. Hutchinson's sign - involvement of the tip of the nose, the nasociliary branch of V1 - predicts globe involvement in about 75% of cases. This man's midline-respecting V1 rash with nasal tip vesicles, pseudodendrite and corneal hypoesthesia fits that description, and he needs an oral antiviral immediately.

optionExplanations.a: The classic form of HSV infectious epithelial keratitis is a dendritic lesion with terminal end bulbs that stains with fluorescein, not a dermatomal V1 vesicular rash with Hutchinson's sign.
optionExplanations.c: A corneal abrasion is acute and commonly follows trauma, and the cornea stays clear; it does not produce a dermatomal facial rash or corneal hypoesthesia.
optionExplanations.d: An ulcer is subacute with a white, necrotic corneal area, obscured iris detail and extension into stroma; corneal ulceration here would be a complication, not the presenting diagnosis.
optionExplanations.e: Chronic interstitial keratitis is listed as a complication of virus penetrating into the stroma, not the acute dermatomal presentation described.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman reports 2 years of gradually worsening drooping of the right upper eyelid, now blocking her superior field. There is no diplopia and no variability through the day, and the pupils are equal. The right lid shows 3 mm of ptosis with a high lid crease, and levator function is normal at 12 mm. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Surgery for ptosis is selected by the amount of ptosis and the levator function: mild ptosis (<2 mm) with normal levator function is treated by Müller-conjunctival resection (Putterman) or tarso-müller-conjunctival resection (Fasanella-Servat); >2 mm ptosis with normal levator function by levator advancement; >2 mm with moderate levator function (4-10 mm of levator function) by levator resection; and >2 mm with severe levator function (<4 mm) by frontalis suspension. This woman has painless, gradually progressive aponeurotic ptosis of 3 mm with normal levator function, so levator advancement is the indicated procedure.

optionExplanations.a: Müller-conjunctival resection (Putterman) is reserved for mild ptosis under 2 mm with normal levator function, and her ptosis is 3 mm.
optionExplanations.c: Levator resection is for >2 mm ptosis with moderate levator function of 4-10 mm, whereas her levator function is normal at 12 mm.
optionExplanations.d: Frontalis suspension, using materials such as fascia lata or silicone, is for >2 mm ptosis with severe levator function of less than 4 mm.
optionExplanations.e: Tarso-müller-conjunctival resection (Fasanella-Servat) is likewise an option for mild ptosis under 2 mm with normal levator function.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man reports several years of night blindness and progressive loss of peripheral vision, and he frequently bumps into objects to his side. A younger brother has the same complaints. Central acuity is 20/25 in each eye. Fundoscopy shows bone-spicule pigment clumping in the mid-periphery of the retina, narrowed retinal arterioles, and a pale optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is a hereditary degenerative disease of the retina in which photoreceptors degenerate (rods more than cones), producing night blindness, decreased peripheral vision ("tunnel vision") and glare. Its fundoscopic triad is areas of bone-spicule pigment clumping in the mid-periphery, narrowed retinal arterioles, and optic disc pallor. This patient has exactly that triad with an affected sibling, fitting the commonly autosomal recessive inheritance of the disease.

optionExplanations.b: Dry AMD is a disease of increasing age marked by drusen between the RPE and Bruch's membrane and geographic atrophy, with slowly progressive loss of central rather than peripheral vision.
optionExplanations.c: Wet AMD is caused by choroidal neovascularization with subretinal hemorrhage and lipid exudate, and causes severe central vision loss, not years of night blindness with bone-spicule pigmentation.
optionExplanations.d: Rhegmatogenous detachment follows a retinal tear and causes abrupt flashes, floaters and a field defect, not a slowly progressive bilateral degeneration with arteriolar narrowing and disc pallor.
optionExplanations.e: Exudative detachment reflects an underlying disease causing subretinal fluid and is managed nonsurgically; it does not produce mid-peripheral bone-spicule pigment clumping.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a baseball. He has diplopia on upgaze with restriction of extraocular movement, and paresthesia of the right cheek and upper lip. Visual acuity is 20/20, the pupil is normal, and the anterior chamber is deep and clear without hyphema. CT of the orbits shows a fracture of about 20% of the orbital floor without muscle incarceration and no enophthalmos. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Immediate surgical repair of the orbital floor
Advise avoidance of coughing, nose blowing and Valsalva maneuvers, and follow the diplopia for improvement
Apply a rigid eye shield, keep him NPO, check tetanus status and start IV cefazolin and an aminoglycoside
Bedrest with minimal exertion and the head of the bed elevated for 5 days
Surgical drainage of the anterior chamber

questions.explanation: In a blow-out fracture the orbital floor fractures and orbital contents herniate into the maxillary sinus while the orbital rim stays intact; diplopia with restricted extraocular movement and infraorbital nerve paresthesia of the cheek and upper lip are classic. The source directs patients to avoid coughing, blowing the nose and Valsalva maneuvers, and reserves surgery for a fracture involving more than 50% of the orbital floor, diplopia that is not improving, or enophthalmos greater than 2 mm, with surgery delayed if the diplopia improves. This small fracture without enophthalmos meets none of those criteria, so observation with follow-up of the diplopia is appropriate.

optionExplanations.a: Surgery is indicated for a fracture involving more than 50% of the orbital floor, non-improving diplopia, or enophthalmos greater than 2 mm; none is present, and repair may be delayed if diplopia improves.
optionExplanations.c: That is the initial management of a suspected ruptured globe or penetrating trauma; here acuity is normal, the pupil is normal and the anterior chamber is deep and clear.
optionExplanations.d: Shielding with bedrest and head-of-bed elevation for 5 days is the treatment of a hyphema, and there is no blood in the anterior chamber.
optionExplanations.e: Surgical drainage is considered for a hyphema that persists or re-bleeds, which this patient does not have.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman has 3 days of pain, swelling and redness below the medial canthus of the left eye, with constant tearing, crusting of the lashes and a low-grade fever. Digital pressure over the swelling expresses pus through the punctum. Visual acuity is 20/25, the cornea is clear, the conjunctiva is only mildly injected, and extraocular movements are full and painless. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dacryocystitis is acute or chronic infection of the lacrimal sac, most commonly due to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, and gram-positive bacteria such as S. aureus and S. pneumoniae are the usual cause in adults. The source describes pain, swelling and redness over the lacrimal sac below the medial canthus, with epiphora, crusting and possible fever, and notes that digital pressure on the lacrimal sac may express pus through the punctum. This patient has every one of those features with a clear cornea and quiet globe, so the infection is localized to the lacrimal sac.

optionExplanations.b: Dacryoadenitis is inflammation of the lacrimal gland in the outer third of the upper eyelid, so the pain, swelling and redness are in the outer region of the upper lid rather than below the medial canthus.
optionExplanations.c: In the chronic form epiphora may be the only symptom of nasolacrimal duct obstruction; uncomplicated obstruction does not produce a tender red swelling with fever and reflux of pus.
optionExplanations.d: Conjunctivitis is an inflammatory cause of epiphora, but it produces diffuse conjunctival injection and discharge rather than a localized tender swelling over the lacrimal sac that expresses pus through the punctum.
optionExplanations.e: Keratitis is another inflammatory cause of reflexive tearing, but it involves the cornea, which is clear here, and would not cause purulent reflux from the punctum.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman who has been nearsighted since her teens reports 6 months of increasing difficulty reading small print. She has found that she can read comfortably only by removing her distance glasses. Distance vision with those glasses is unchanged at 20/20, the eyes are white and quiet, the lenses are clear, and fundoscopy is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the normal aging process from about age 40 in which hardening and reduced deformability of the lens decrease accommodative ability, so near images cannot be focused onto the retina and accommodative power falls from about 14 D at age 10 to 3.5 D by age 40. The source states that a person who is initially myopic removes their distance glasses to read, which is precisely this patient's adaptation, and her distance vision is unaffected. Correction is with positive diopter, convex, "plus" lenses for reading.

optionExplanations.b: Hyperopia is a globe too short relative to its refractive mechanisms; it makes symptoms of presbyopia occur earlier rather than explaining them, and this patient is myopic with unchanged distance acuity.
optionExplanations.c: Anisometropia is a difference in refractive error between the eyes; her complaint is symmetric and confined to near vision, and her distance correction still gives 20/20.
optionExplanations.d: Regular astigmatism is non-uniform refraction from a non-spherical cornea or lens and causes blurry vision, squinting, asthenopia or headaches at distance as well as near, not isolated loss of near focus.
optionExplanations.e: Myopia usually presents in the 1st or 2nd decade and stabilizes in the 2nd and 3rd, rarely beginning after age 25 except with DM hyperglycemia or early nuclear sclerotic cataracts; her lenses are clear and her distance vision has not changed.
